title: Positive or Negative?
theme: Connotation: how a word feels, not just what it means
objectives: I can explain how two words with similar meanings can feel positive or negative.
I can choose the word that fits a person's actions and my opinion of them.
I can use ten describing words in a story, a discussion, and a short argument.
I can tell the difference between being bold and being foolish.
rationale: Grade 5 begins with connotation because every later unit asks students to choose words deliberately. Five pairs (frugal/stingy, inquisitive/nosy, assertive/bossy, daring/foolhardy, easygoing/idle) show the same behavior wearing a positive or negative label. The unit builds the habit of asking not only what a word means but how it makes a reader feel about a person, which supports character analysis, debate, and writing with a point of view.

words.def: Careful about spending money and not wasting things.
words.ex: The frugal family packed lunches at home and saved the money for a camping trip.
words.ex2: Being frugal with paper, Ines used both sides of every sheet.
words.nonExample: Buying a new gadget every week is not a frugal habit.

apps.spoken: We are being frugal this month, so we are cooking at home.
apps.writing: Use frugal to praise smart saving; the word has a positive feeling.

words.ex2: I felt nosy for asking, but I wanted to know who had called her.
words.nonExample: Asking a teacher how a volcano works is curious, not nosy.

cloze2.s: Mr. Lee said he did not mean to be ___, but he asked three times how much we paid for the house.

misuse.s: The nosy girl respected her friend's privacy and never looked at her diary.

words.def: Speaking up for your needs or ideas in a firm, polite way.

words.def: Bold in a silly way that ignores real danger.
words.ex: It was foolhardy to swim in the river right after the storm raised the water.
words.ex2: The foolhardy driver sped around the sharp curve with his lights off.
words.nonExample: Wearing a helmet and testing the ice before skating is the opposite of foolhardy.

words.def: Calm and relaxed; not easily upset or worried.
words.ex: My easygoing uncle just laughed when the pancakes burned and made toast instead.
words.ex2: On long bus trips, easygoing teammates keep everyone's mood light.

morph.note: A compound word made of two words.

apps.writing: Use easygoing for a character who stays calm when plans change.

words.def: Not working or being used; doing nothing.

passage.title: The Garage Sale
paras: When the Rivera twins planned a garage sale, their grandmother offered to help. She was frugal, a woman who saved every jar and button, and she knew how to price things fairly. Tomás was easygoing and happy to carry boxes, while his sister Luz was assertive and explained the plan in a firm, polite voice.

Early on Saturday, Mr. Hale arrived. He was inquisitive about everything and asked who had built the old radio. Another visitor was nosy. She kept asking how much money the twins' parents earned, until Luz said, "That is private."

By noon the sale was slow, and Tomás sat idle, balancing a broom on his chin. Their friend Dev, who tended to be bossy, shouted that everyone must follow his plan: sell lemonade in the middle of the street. His idea was daring, but Grandmother shook her head. "Standing in traffic is foolhardy," she said. "Use the sidewalk."

Later, a shopper bargained hard over a lamp. "What a stingy man," Dev whispered. Grandmother disagreed. "He is being frugal, not stingy," she said. "He is watching his money, and he is paying a fair price." Luz smiled. She realized that one behavior can earn two different words, and the word you choose shows how you feel about the person.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "nosy" describes a person who is
qs.why: The visitor asks about the family's income, a private matter, so nosy means too curious about private things.

qs.q: Why does Grandmother say the shopper is frugal and not stingy?
choices: He wants to take the lamp without paying.
He is angry at the twins.
He is careful with money but still pays a fair price.
qs.why: A stingy person refuses to give what is fair; this shopper pays a fair price, so frugal fits better.

qs.q: Which detail from paragraph 3 best explains why Grandmother called Dev's plan foolhardy?
choices: The lemonade stand would be in the middle of the street, where cars pass.
Tomás sat idle by the table.
The sale was slow at noon.
qs.why: A stand in traffic is a real danger, which is why the plan is foolhardy and not just daring.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Two words can describe similar behavior but change how we feel about a person.
qs.why: Luz's final realization states the idea: word choice shows our feeling about someone.

constructed.prompt: Two people each save money, but one shares and the other does not. Describe them with frugal and stingy and name the action that makes each word fit.
look: names a concrete action for each
constructed.model: Rosa is frugal: she brings lunch from home and saves for a bike, but she still buys a gift for her friend. Her cousin is stingy: he has plenty of money and still refuses to share his snacks.

look: explains the line between learning and prying

teacher.overview: Students learn ten describing words organized as pairs that share an idea but differ in feeling (connotation). They use the words in a narrative, discussion, and short argument, and they practice choosing the word that matches both the facts and their opinion.

notes.va.frugal.adj: Positive word for careful saving. Pair with stingy on a two-column chart: same facts, different feeling. Ask what a frugal person does with the money they save.
notes.va.stingy.adj: Negative word: holding back what one could share. Students often use stingy for any saver; stress that the difference is willingness to share, not the amount saved.
notes.va.inquisitive.adj: Positive curiosity about ideas and how things work. Model with questions about science, then contrast with nosy.
notes.va.nosy.adj: Curiosity about private matters. Use a sort: which questions are about learning and which are about privacy? Avoid examples about students' families.
notes.va.assertive.adj: Firm and polite. Model the sentence 'I would like a turn' and compare it with a shout and with silence. Notice the suffix -ive on assert.
notes.va.bossy.adj: Giving orders and ignoring others. Contrast with assertive: both speak up, but only bossy ignores other people's ideas.
notes.va.daring.adj: Positive: brave with a purpose. Ask students to name a daring act that is also well planned.
notes.va.foolhardy.adj: Bravery without sense. Point out the two parts, fool and hardy (bold). Use it for an action, not as an insult for a person.
notes.va.easygoing.adj: A compound: easy + going. Usually positive, but ask when being too easygoing could cause trouble.
notes.va.idle.adj: Two feelings: neutral for machines or places not in use, critical when used for a person who seems lazy. Ask students to say who is speaking and what they feel.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'Two people save money. The first brings lunch and still buys a birthday gift. That is careful, so I choose frugal. The second has plenty and will not share even a snack. That is holding back, so stingy fits. The facts are different, and so are the feelings the words give me.'
discuss: Which word would you want a friend to use about you, assertive or bossy? Why?
How can the same action be called daring by one person and foolhardy by another?
misconceptions: Stingy and frugal mean exactly the same thing.
Nosy is just a stronger word for inquisitive.
extend: Collect a pair of words for the same behavior from a book or article and explain which one the author chose and why.
Rewrite a short paragraph about a character so that the same actions sound positive, then negative.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit the pairs two days later in a quick sort (positive or negative), again at one week, and connect them to ambitious, thrifty, and sensible from grade 4. Use them again in the debate vocabulary of unit 2.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (tacaño, entrometido, temerario, ocioso, mandón, tranquilo, audaz) not reviewed by a native speaker; regional variation is likely for tacaño and mandón.
Sense boundary of idle: taught as 'not working or not in use' with a note that it can sound critical when used about a person.
foolhardy: second part 'hardy' glossed as 'bold' (from Old French hardi); confirm the gloss suits grade 5 readers.
